question: Three young brother-sister pairs from different families need to take a trip in a van. These six children will occupy the second and third rows in the van, each of which has three seats. To avoid disruptions, siblings may not sit right next to each other in the same row, and no child may sit directly in front of his or her sibling. How many seating arrangements are possible for this trip?
solution:
First count the family occupying each seat, then distinguish the two siblings within each family. Read both rows from left to right.

Suppose a row contains both siblings from one family, labeled \(X\). They must occupy the two end seats, so the row has pattern \(XYX\). The other row then contains one \(Y\) and two \(Z\)'s. To keep the \(Z\) siblings apart, that row must be \(ZYZ\). But the \(Y\) siblings would be directly in front of one another. Thus every valid row contains one child from each family.

There are \(3!=6\) ways to order the families in the second row. Label that order \(XYZ\). The third row also contains one of each letter, with no letter in the same column as its sibling.

Its left seat must be \(Y\) or \(Z\). If it is \(Y\), the right seat must be \(X\), giving \(YZX\). If it is \(Z\), the middle seat must be \(X\), giving \(ZXY\). Both patterns satisfy all restrictions.

For each family, either sibling can occupy its assigned second-row seat, giving \(2^3=8\) choices. Every seating uniquely determines its family orders and sibling placements, so these choices introduce no duplicates. The total is
\[
6\cdot2\cdot8=\boxed{96},
\]
choice \(\text{D}\).
